entries.9420fc59df22f5052a8c28566db28cd4c31ab9b2: <div sID="gen3124" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Num.22" sID="Num.22"/> <div eID="gen3124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3125" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3126" type="x-p"/> At this chapter begins the famous story of Balak and Balaam, their attempt to curse Israel, and the baffling of that attempt; God's people are long afterwards told to remember what Balak the king of Moab consulted, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him, that they might know the righteousness of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.5">Mic. vi. 5</reference>. In this chapter we have, I. Balak's fear of Israel, and the plot he had to get them cursed, <reference osisRef="Num.22.1-Num.22.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The embassy he sent to Balaam, a conjurer, to fetch him for that purpose, and the disappointment he met with in the first embassy, <reference osisRef="Num.22.5-Num.22.14">ver. 5-14</reference>. III. Balaam's coming to him upon his second message, <reference osisRef="Num.22.15-Num.22.21">ver. 15-21</reference>. IV. The opposition Balaam met with by the way, <reference osisRef="Num.22.22-Num.22.35">ver. 22-35</reference>. V. The interview at length between Balak and Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.22.36-Num.22.41">ver. 36</reference>, &c.
entries.442d767a8b67d5188d58c84065d3dbbc38530fd8: <div eID="gen3126" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3125" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Balak Sends for Balaam. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3127" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the children of Israel set forward, and pitched in the plains of Moab on this side Jordan <hi type="italic">by</hi> Jericho. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Balak the son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorites. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Moab was sore afraid of the people, because they <hi type="italic">were</hi> many: and Moab was distressed because of the children of Israel. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Moab said unto the elders of Midian, Now shall this company lick up all <hi type="italic">that are</hi> round about us, as the ox licketh up the grass of the field. And Balak the son of Zippor <hi type="italic">was</hi> king of the Moabites at that time. <hi type="super">5</hi> He sent messengers therefore unto Balaam the son of Beor to Pethor, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by the river of the land of the children of his people, to call him, saying, Behold, there is a people come out from Egypt: behold, they cover the face of the earth, and they abide over against me: <hi type="super">6</hi> Come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people; for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> too mighty for me: peradventure I shall prevail, <hi type="italic">that</hi> we may smite them, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> I may drive them out of the land: for I wot that he whom thou blessest <hi type="italic">is</hi> blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian departed with the rewards of divination in their hand; and they came unto Balaam, and spake unto him the words of Balak. 8 And he said unto them, Lodge here this night, and I will bring you word again, as the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall speak unto me: and the princes of Moab abode with Balaam. 9 And God came unto Balaam, and said, What men <hi type="italic">are</hi> these with thee? <hi type="super">10</hi> And Balaam said unto God, Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, hath sent unto me, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a people come out of Egypt, which covereth the face of the earth: come now, curse me them; peradventure I shall be able to overcome them, and drive them out. 12 And God said unto Balaam, Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> blessed. 13 And Balaam rose up in the morning, and said unto the princes of Balak, Get you into your land: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> refuseth to give me leave to go with you. 14 And the princes of Moab rose up, and they went unto Balak, and said, Balaam refuseth to come with us. <div eID="gen3127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3128" type="x-p"/> The children of Israel have at length finished their wanderings in the wilderness, out of which they went up (<reference osisRef="Num.21.18">ch. xxi. 18</reference>), and are now encamped in the plains of Moab near Jordan, where they continued till they passed through Jordan under Joshua, after the death of Moses. Now we have here, <div eID="gen3128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3129" type="x-p"/> I. The fright which the Moabites were in upon the approach of Israel, <reference osisRef="Num.22.2-Num.22.4">v. 2-4</reference>. They needed not to fear any harm from them if they knew (and it is probable that Moses let them know) the orders God had given to Israel not to contend with the Moabites, nor to use any hostility against them, <reference osisRef="Deut.2.9">Deut. ii. 9</reference>. But, if they had any notice of this, they were jealous that it was but a sham, to make them secure, that they might be the more easily conquered. Notwithstanding the old friendship between Abraham and Lot, the Moabites resolved to ruin Israel if they could, and therefore they will take it for granted, without any ground for the suspicion, that Israel resolves to ruin them. Thus it is common for those that design mischief to pretend that mischief is designed against them; and their groundless jealousies must be the colour of their causeless malice. They hear of their triumphs over the Amorites (<reference osisRef="Num.22.2">v. 2</reference>), and think that their own house is in danger when their neighbour's is on fire. They observe their multitudes (<reference osisRef="Num.22.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They were many;</hi> and hence infer how easily they would conquer their country, and all about them if some speedy and effectual course were not taken to stop the progress of their victorious arms: "They shall <hi type="italic">lick up</hi> or devour us, and <hi type="italic">all that are round about us,</hi> as speedily and irresistibly <hi type="italic">as the ox eats up the grass</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Num.22.4">v. 4</reference>), owning themselves to be an unequal match for so formidable an enemy. Therefore they were sorely afraid and distressed themselves; thus were the wicked <hi type="italic">in great fear where no fear was,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.53.5">Ps. liii. 5</reference>. These fears they communicated to their neighbours, the elders of Midian, that some measures might be concerted between them for their common safety; for, if the kingdom of Moab fall, the republic of Midian cannot stand long. The Moabites, if they had pleased, might have made a good use of the advances of Israel, and their successes against the Amorites. They had reason to rejoice, and give God and Israel thanks for freeing them from the threatening power of Sihon king of the Amorites, who had taken from them part of their country, and was likely to overrun the rest. They had reason likewise to court Israel's friendship, and to come in to their assistance; but having forsaken the religion of their father Lot, and being sunk into idolatry, they hated the people of the God of Abraham, and were justly infatuated in their counsels and given up to distress. <div eID="gen3129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3130" type="x-p"/> II. The project which the king of Moab formed to get the people of Israel cursed, that is, to set God against them, who, he perceived, hitherto fought for them. He trusted more to his arts than to his arms, and had a notion that if he could but get some prophet or other, with his powerful charms, to imprecate evil upon them, and to pronounce a blessing upon himself and his forces, then, though otherwise too weak, he should be able to deal with them. This notion arose, 1. Out of the remains of some religion; for it owns a dependence upon some visible sovereign powers that rule in the affairs of the children of men and determine them, and an obligation upon us to make application to these powers. 2. Out of the ruins of the true religion; for if the Midianites and Moabites had not wretchedly degenerated from the faith and worship of their pious ancestors, Abraham and Lot, they could not have imagined it possible to do any mischief with their curses to a people who alone adhered to the service of the true God, from whose service they had themselves revolted. <div eID="gen3130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3131" type="x-p"/> III. The court which he made to Balaam the son of Beor, a famous conjurer, to engage him to curse Israel. The Balaam lived a great way off, in that country whence Abraham came, and where Laban lived; but, though it was probable that there were many nearer home that were pretenders to divination, yet none had so great a reputation for success as Balaam, and Balak will employ the best he can hear of, though he send a great way for him, so much is his heart upon this project. And to gain him, 1. He makes him his friend, complaining to him, as his confidant, of the danger he was in from the numbers and neighbourhood of the camp of Israel: <hi type="italic">They cover the face of the earth,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">abide over against me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.5">v. 5</reference>. 2. In effect he makes him his god, by the great power he attributes to his word: <hi type="italic">He whom thou blessest is blessed,</hi> and <hi type="italic">he whom thou cursest is cursed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.6">v. 6</reference>. The learned bishop Patrick inclines to think, with many of the Jewish writers, that Balaam had been a great prophet, who, for the accomplishment of his predictions and the answers of his prayers, both for good and evil, had been looked upon justly as a man of great interest with God; but that, growing proud and covetous, God departed from him, and then, to support his sinking credit, he betook himself to diabolical arts. He is called a <hi type="italic">prophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.16">2 Pet. ii. 16</reference>,) because he had been one, or perhaps he had raised his reputation from the first by his magical charms, as Simon Magus, who bewitched the people so far that he was called <hi type="italic">the great power of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.8.10">Acts viii. 10</reference>. Curses pronounced by God's prophets in the name of the Lord have wonderful effects, as Noah's (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Gen. ix. 25</reference>), and Elisha's, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.24">2 Kings ii. 24</reference>. But the curse <hi type="italic">causeless shall not come</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.26.2">Prov. xxvi. 2</reference>), no more than Goliath's, when he <hi type="italic">cursed David by his gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.43">1 Sam. xvii. 43</reference>. Let us desire to have the prayers of God's ministers and people for us, and dread having them against us; for they are greatly regarded by him who blesseth indeed and curseth indeed. But Balak cannot rely upon these compliments as sufficient to prevail with Balaam, the main inducement is yet behind (<reference osisRef="Num.22.7">v. 7</reference>): they took <hi type="italic">the rewards of divination in their hand, the wages of unrighteousness,</hi> which he <hi type="italic">loved,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15">2 Pet. ii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen3131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3132" type="x-p"/> IV. The restraint God lays upon Balaam, forbidding him to curse Israel. It is very probable that Balaam, being a curious inquisitive man, was no stranger to Israel's case and character, but had heard that God was with them of a truth, so that he ought to have given the messengers their answer immediately, that he would never curse a people whom God had blessed; but he lodges the messengers, and takes a night's time to consider what he shall do, and to receive instructions from God, <reference osisRef="Num.22.8">v. 8</reference>. When we enter into a parley with temptations we are in great danger of being overcome by them. In the night God comes to him, probably in a dream, and enquires what business those strangers had with him. He knows it, but he will know it from him. Balaam gives him an account of their errand (<reference osisRef="Num.22.9-Num.22.11">v. 9-11</reference>), and God thereupon charges him not to go with them, or attempt to curse that blessed people, <reference osisRef="Num.22.12">v. 12</reference>. Thus God sometimes, for the preservation of his people, was pleased to speak to bad men, as to Abimelech (<reference osisRef="Gen.20.3">Gen. xx. 3</reference>), and to Laban, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.24">Gen. xxxi. 24</reference>. And we read of some that were workers of iniquity, and yet in Christ's name prophesied, and <hi type="italic">did many wondrous works.</hi> Balaam is charged not only not to go to Balak, but not to offer to curse this people, which he might have attempted at a distance; and the reason is given: <hi type="italic">They are blessed.</hi> This was part of the blessing of Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Gen. xii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will curse him that curseth thee;</hi> so that an attempt to curse them would be not only fruitless, but perilous. Israel had often provoked God in the wilderness, yet he will not suffer their enemies to curse them, for he <hi type="italic">rewards them not according to their iniquities.</hi> The blessedness of those whose sin is covered comes upon them, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.6-Rom.4.7">Rom. iv. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen3132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3133" type="x-p"/> V. The return of the messengers without Balaam. 1. Balaam is not faithful in returning God's answer to the messengers, <reference osisRef="Num.22.13">v. 13</reference>. He only tells them, <hi type="italic">the Lord refuseth to give me leave to go with you.</hi> He did not tell them, as he ought to have done, that Israel was a blessed people, and must by no means be cursed; for then the design would have been crushed, and the temptation would not have been renewed: but he, in effect, desired them to give his humble service to Balak, and let him know that he applauded his project, and would have been very glad to gratify him, but that truly he had the character of a prophet, and must not go without leave from God, which he had not yet obtained, and therefore for the present he must be excused. Note, Those are a fair mark for Satan's temptation that speak diminishingly of divine prohibitions, as if they amounted to no more than the denial of a permission, and as if to go against God's law were only to go without his leave. 2. The messengers are not faithful in returning Balaam's answer to Balak. All the account they give of it is, <hi type="italic">Balaam refuseth to come with us</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.22.14">v. 14</reference>), intimating that he only wanted more courtship and higher proffers; but they are not willing Balak should know that God had signified his disallowance of the attempt. Thus are great men wretchedly abused by the flatteries of those about them, who do all they can to prevent their seeing their own faults and follies.
entries.2ba2b78217728af97e3951affc9b803df0c58032: <div eID="gen3133" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Balak's Second Message to Balaam. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3134" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Balak sent yet again princes, more, and more honourable than they. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they came to Balaam, and said to him, Thus saith Balak the son of Zippor, Let nothing, I pray thee, hinder thee from coming unto me: <hi type="super">17</hi> For I will promote thee unto very great honour, and I will do whatsoever thou sayest unto me: come therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people. 18 And Balaam answered and said unto the servants of Balak, If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God, to do less or more. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now therefore, I pray you, tarry ye also here this night, that I may know what the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will say unto me more. <hi type="super">20</hi> And God came unto Balaam at night, and said unto him, If the men come to call thee, rise up, <hi type="italic">and</hi> go with them; but yet the word which I shall say unto thee, that shalt thou do. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Balaam rose up in the morning, and saddled his ass, and went with the princes of Moab. <div eID="gen3134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3135" type="x-p"/> We have here a second embassy sent to Balaam, to fetch him over to curse Israel. It were well for us if we were as earnest and constant in prosecuting a good work, notwithstanding disappointments, as Balak was in pursuing this ill design. The enemies of the church are restless and unwearied in their attempts against it; but he that sits in heaven laughs at them. Observe, <div eID="gen3135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3136" type="x-p"/> I. The temptation Balak laid before Balaam. He contrived to make this assault more vigorous than the former. It is very probable that he sent double money in the hands of his messengers; but, besides that, now he tempted him with honours, laid a bait not only for his covetousness, but for his pride and ambition. How earnestly should we beg of God daily to mortify in us these two limbs of the old man! Those that know how to look with a holy contempt upon worldly wealth and preferment will find it not so hard a matter as most men do to keep a good conscience. See how artfully Balak managed the temptation. 1. The messengers he sent were <hi type="italic">more,</hi> and <hi type="italic">more honourable,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.15">v. 15</reference>. He sent to this conjurer with as great respect and deference to his quality as if he had been a sovereign prince, apprehending perhaps that Balaam had thought himself slighted in the fewness and meanness of the former messengers. 2. The request was very urgent. This powerful prince becomes a suitor to him: "<hi type="italic">Let nothing, I pray thee, hinder thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.22.16">v. 16</reference>), no, not God, nor conscience, nor any fear either of sin or shame." 3. The proffers were high: "<hi type="italic">I will promote thee to very great honour</hi> among the princes of Moab;" nay, he gives him a blank, and he shall write his own terms: <hi type="italic">I will do whatsoever thou sayest,</hi> that is, "I will give thee whatever thou desirest, and observe whatever thou orderest; thy word shall be a law to me," <reference osisRef="Num.22.17">v. 17</reference>. Thus sinners stick at no pains, spare no cost, and care not how low they stoop, for the gratifying either of their luxury or of their malice; shall we then be stiff and strait-handed in our compliance with the laws of virtue? God forbid. <div eID="gen3136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3137" type="x-p"/> II. Balaam's seeming resistance of, but real yielding to, this temptation. We may here discern in Balaam a struggle between his convictions and his corruptions. 1. His convictions charged him to adhere to the command of God, and he spoke their language, <reference osisRef="Num.22.18">v. 18</reference>. Nor could any man have said better: "<hi type="italic">If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold,</hi> and that is more than he can give or I can ask, <hi type="italic">I cannot go beyond the word of the Lord my God.</hi>" See how honourably he speaks of God; he is <hi type="italic">Jehovah, my God.</hi> Note, Many call God theirs that are not his, not <hi type="italic">truly</hi> because not <hi type="italic">only</hi> his; <hi type="italic">they swear by the Lord, and by Malcham.</hi> See how respectfully he speaks of the word of God, as one resolved to stick to it, and in nothing to vary from it, and how slightly of the wealth of this world, as if gold and silver were nothing to him in comparison with the favour of God; and yet, at the same time, the searcher of hearts knew that he loved the wages of unrighteousness. Note, It is an easy thing for bad men to speak very good words, and with their mouth to make a show of piety. There is no judging of men by their words. God knows the heart. 2. His corruptions at the same time strongly inclined him to go contrary to the command. He seemed to refuse the temptation, <reference osisRef="Num.22.18">v. 18</reference>. But even then he expressed no abhorrence of it, as Christ did when he had the kingdoms of the world offered him (<hi type="italic">Get thee hence Satan</hi>), and as Peter did when Simon Magus offered him money: <hi type="italic">Thy money perish with thee.</hi> But it appears (<reference osisRef="Num.22.19">v. 19</reference>) that he had a strong inclination to accept the proffer; for he would further attend, to know what God would say to him, hoping that he might alter his mind and give him leave to go. This was a vile reflection upon God Almighty, as if he could change his mind, and now at last suffer those to be cursed whom he had pronounced blessed, and as if he would be brought to allow what he had already declared to be evil. Surely he thought God <hi type="italic">altogether such a one as himself.</hi> He had already been told what the will of God was, in which he ought to have acquiesced, and not to have desired a re-hearing of that cause which was already so plainly determined. Note, It is a very great affront to God, and a certain evidence of the dominion of corruption in the heart, to beg leave to sin. <div eID="gen3137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3138" type="x-p"/> III. The permission God gave him to go, <reference osisRef="Num.22.20">v. 20</reference>. God came to him, probably by an anger, and told him he might, if he pleased, go with Balak's messengers. <hi type="italic">So he gave him up to his own heart's lust.</hi> "Since thou hast such a mind to go, even go, yet know that <hi type="italic">the journey thou undertakest shall not be for thy honour;</hi> for, though thou hast leave to go, thou shalt not, as thou hopest, have leave to curse, <hi type="italic">for the word which I shall say unto thee, that thou shalt do.</hi>" Note, God has wicked men in a chain; <hi type="italic">hitherto they shall come</hi> by his permission, but no further that he does permit them. Thus he makes the wrath of man to praise him, yet, at the same time, restrains the remainder of it. It was in anger that God said to Balaam, "Go with them," and we have reason to think that Balaam himself so understood it, for we do not find him pleading this allowance when God reproved him for going. Note, As God sometimes denies the prayers of his people in love, so sometimes he grants the desires of the wicked in wrath. <div eID="gen3138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3139" type="x-p"/> IV. His setting out in the journey, <reference osisRef="Num.22.21">v. 21</reference>. God gave him leave to go <hi type="italic">if the men called him,</hi> but he was so fond of the journey that we do not find he staid for their calling him, but he himself <hi type="italic">rose up in the morning,</hi> got every thing ready with all speed, and <hi type="italic">went with the princes of Moab,</hi> who were proud enough that they had carried their point. The apostle describes Balaam's sin here to be that he <hi type="italic">ran greedily into an error for reward,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.11">Jude 11</reference>. The love of money is the root of all evil.
entries.fe9d08d5c7958a39d3cb6186f538009560e1f9bd: <div eID="gen3139" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Displeasure against Balaam; Remonstrance of Balaam's Ass; The Angel Appears to Balaam. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3140" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And God's anger was kindled because he went: and the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stood in the way for an adversary against him. Now he was riding upon his ass, and his two servants <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the ass saw the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand: and the ass turned aside out of the way, and went into the field: and Balaam smote the ass, to turn her into the way. <hi type="super">24</hi> But the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stood in a path of the vineyards, a wall <hi type="italic">being</hi> on this side, and a wall on that side. <hi type="super">25</hi> And when the ass saw the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , she thrust herself unto the wall, and crushed Balaam's foot against the wall: and he smote her again. 26 And the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> went further, and stood in a narrow place, where <hi type="italic">was</hi> no way to turn either to the right hand or to the left. <hi type="super">27</hi> And when the ass saw the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , she fell down under Balaam: and Balaam's anger was kindled, and he smote the ass with a staff. <hi type="super">28</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> opened the mouth of the ass, and she said unto Balaam, What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me these three times? <hi type="super">29</hi> And Balaam said unto the ass, Because thou hast mocked me: I would there were a sword in mine hand, for now would I kill thee. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the ass said unto Balaam, <hi type="italic">Am</hi> not I thine ass, upon which thou hast ridden ever since <hi type="italic">I was</hi> thine unto this day? was I ever wont to do so unto thee? And he said, Nay. <hi type="super">31</hi> Then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> opened the eyes of Balaam, and he saw the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand: and he bowed down his head, and fell flat on his face. <hi type="super">32</hi> And the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto him, Wherefore hast thou smitten thine ass these three times? behold, I went out to withstand thee, because <hi type="italic">thy</hi> way is perverse before me: 33 And the ass saw me, and turned from me these three times: unless she had turned from me, surely now also I had slain thee, and saved her alive. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Balaam said unto the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I have sinned; for I knew not that thou stoodest in the way against me: now therefore, if it displease thee, I will get me back again. <hi type="super">35</hi> And the angel of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto Balaam, Go with the men: but only the word that I shall speak unto thee, that thou shalt speak. So Balaam went with the princes of Balak. <div eID="gen3140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3141" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the opposition God gave to Balaam in his journey towards Moab; probably the princes had gone before, or gone some other way, and Balaam had pointed out where he would meet them, or where they should stay for him, for we read nothing of them in this part of our narrative, only that Balaam, like a person of some quality, was attended with his two men-honour enough, one would think, for such a man, he needed not be beholden to Balak for promotion. <div eID="gen3141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3142" type="x-p"/> I. Here is God's displeasure against Balaam for undertaking this journey: God's <hi type="italic">anger was kindled because he went,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.22">v. 22</reference>. Note, 1. The sin of sinners is not to be thought the less provoking to God because he permits it. We must not think that, because God does not by his providence restrain men from sin, therefore he approves of it, or that it is therefore not hateful to him; he suffers sin, and yet is angry at it. 2. Nothing is more displeasing to God than malicious designs against his people; he that touches them touches the apple of his eye. <div eID="gen3142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3143" type="x-p"/> II. The way God took to let Balaam know his displeasure against him: <hi type="italic">An angel stood in the way for an adversary.</hi> Now God fulfilled his promise to Israel (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.22">Exod. xxiii. 22</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will be an enemy to thy enemies.</hi> The holy angels are adversaries to sin, and perhaps are employed more than we are aware of in preventing it, particularly in opposing those that have any ill designs against God's church and people, for whom Michael our prince stands up, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Dan. xii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">x. 21</reference>. What a comfort is this to all that wish well to the Israel of God, that he never suffers wicked men to form an attempt against them, without sending his holy angels forth to break the attempt and secure his little ones! When the prophet saw the four horns that scattered Judah, at the same time he saw four carpenters that were to fray those horns, <reference osisRef="Zech.1.18-Zech.1.21">Zech. i. 18</reference>, &c. When the <hi type="italic">enemy comes in like a flood the Spirit of the Lord will lift up a standard against him.</hi> This angel was an adversary to Balaam, because Balaam counted him his adversary; otherwise those are really our best friends, and we are so to reckon them, that stop our progress in a sinful way. The angel stood with his sword drawn (<reference osisRef="Num.22.23">v. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">a flaming sword,</hi> like that in the hands of the cherubim (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.24">Gen. iii. 24</reference>), <hi type="italic">turning every way.</hi> Note, The holy angels are at war with those with whom God is angry, for they are the ministers of his justice. Observe, <div eID="gen3143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3144" type="x-p"/> 1. Balaam had notice given him of God's displeasure, by the ass, and this <hi type="italic">did not startle him.</hi> The <hi type="italic">ass saw the angel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.23">v. 23</reference>. How vainly did Balaam boast that he was a man whose <hi type="italic">eyes were open,</hi> and that he <hi type="italic">saw the visions of the Almighty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.24.3-Num.24.4">ch. xxiv. 3, 4</reference>), when the ass he rode on saw more than he did, his eyes being blinded with covetousness and ambition and dazzled with the rewards of divination! Note, Many have God against them, and his holy angels, but are not aware of it. The <hi type="italic">ass knows his owner,</hi> sees his danger, but Balaam does <hi type="italic">not know, does not consider,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lord, when thy hand is lifted up, they will not see,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Isa. xxvi. 11</reference>. Let none be puffed up with a conceit of visions and revelations, when even an ass saw an angel; yet let those be ashamed of their own sottishness, worse than that of the beasts that perish, who, when they are told of the sword of God's wrath drawn against them, while they persist in wicked ways, yet will go on: the ass understood the law of self-preservation better than so; for, to save both herself and her senseless rider, (1.) She <hi type="italic">turned aside out of the way,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.23">v. 23</reference>. Balaam should have taken the hint of this, and considered whether he was not out of the way of his duty; but, instead of this, he <hi type="italic">beat her into the way again.</hi> Thus those who by wilful sin are running headlong into perdition are angry at those that would prevent their ruin. (2.) She had not gone much further before she saw the angel again, and the, to avoid him, <hi type="italic">ran up to a wall,</hi> and <hi type="italic">crushed her rider's foot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.24-Num.22.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. How many ill accidents are we liable to in travelling upon the road, from which if we are preserved we must own our obligations to the divine Providence, which by the ministry of angels <hi type="italic">keeps us in all our ways, lest we dash our foot against a stone;</hi> but, if we at any time meet with a disaster, it should put us upon enquiring whether our way be right in the sight of God or no. The crushing of Balaam's foot, though it was the saving of his life, provoked him so much that he smote his ass the second time, so angry are we apt to be at that which, though a present uneasiness, yet is a real kindness. (3.) Upon the next encounter with the angel, the ass fell down under Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.22.26-Num.22.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. He ought to have considered that there was certainly something extraordinary in this; for his ass was not restive, nor did she use to serve him thus: but it is common for those whose hearts are <hi type="italic">fully set in them to do evil</hi> to push on violently, and break through all the difficulties which Providence lays in their way to give check to them and to stop them in their career. Balaam the third time smote his ass, though she had now done him the best piece of service that ever she did him, saving him from the sword of the angel, and by her falling down teaching him to do likewise. (4.) When all this would not work upon him, God opened the mouth of the ass, and she spoke to him once and again; and yet neither did this move him: <hi type="italic">The Lord opened the mouth of the ass,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.28">v. 28</reference>. This was a great miracle, quite above the power of nature, and wrought by the power of the God of nature, who made man's mouth, and taught him to speak, for otherwise (since we learn to speak purely by imitation, and therefore those that are born deaf are consequently dumb) the first man would never have spoken, nor any of his seed. He that made man speak could, when he pleased, make the ass to <hi type="italic">speak with man's voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.16">2 Pet. ii. 16</reference>. Here Mr. Ainsworth observes that the devil, when he tempted our first parents to sin, employed a subtle serpent, but that God, when he would convince Balaam, employed a silly ass, a creature dull and sottish to a proverb; for Satan corrupts men's minds by the <hi type="italic">craftiness of those that lie in wait to deceive,</hi> but Christ has <hi type="italic">chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise.</hi> By a dumb ass God rebukes the madness of the prophet, for he will never want reprovers, but when he pleases can make the stones cry out as witnesses to him, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.40">Luke xix. 40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">Hab. ii. 11</reference>. [1.] The ass complained of Balaam's cruelty (<reference osisRef="Num.22.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">What have I done unto thee, that thou hast smitten me?</hi> Note, The righteous God will not see the meanest and weakest abused; but either they shall be enabled to speak in their own defence or he will some way or other speak for them. If God would not suffer a beast to be wronged, much less a man, a Christian, a child of his own. We cannot <hi type="italic">open the mouth of the dumb,</hi> as God did here, but we may and must <hi type="italic">open our mouth for the dumb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.8">Prov. xxxi. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.13">Job xxxi. 13</reference>. The ass's complaint was just: <hi type="italic">What have I done?</hi> Note, When we are prompted to smite any with hand or tongue, we should consider what they have done unto us, and what provocation they have given us. We hear it not, but thus the whole creation groans, being burdened, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">Rom. viii. 22</reference>. It was much that Balaam was not astonished to hear his ass speak, and put to confusion: but some think that it was no new thing to him (being a conjurer) to be thus spoken to by his familiars; others rather think that his brutish head-strong passion so blinded him that he could not observe or consider the strangeness of the thing. Nothing besots men worse than unbridled anger. Balaam in his fury <hi type="italic">wished he had a sword to kill his ass with,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.29">v. 29</reference>. See his impotency; can he think by his curses to do mischief to Israel that has it not in his power to kill his own ass? This he cannot do, yet he fain would; and what would he get by that, but make himself so much the poorer (as many do), to gratify his passion and revenge? Such was the madness of this false prophet. Here bishop Hall observes, It is ill falling into the hands of those whom the brute-creatures find unmerciful; for <hi type="italic">a good man regardeth the life of his beast.</hi> [2.] The ass reasoned with him, <reference osisRef="Num.22.30">v. 30</reference>. God enabled not only a dumb creature to speak, but a dull creature to speak to the purpose. Three things she argues with him from:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> His propriety in her: <hi type="italic">Am not I thy ass?</hi> Note, 1. God has given to man a dominion over the creatures: they are <hi type="italic">delivered into his hand</hi> to be used, and <hi type="italic">put under his feet</hi> to be ruled. 2. Even wicked people have a title to the possessions God gives to them, which they are not to be wronged of. 3. The dominion God has given us over the creatures is a good reason why we should not abuse them. We are their lords, and therefore must not be tyrants. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Her serviceableness to him: <hi type="italic">On which thou hast ridden.</hi> Note, It is good for us often to consider how useful the inferior creatures are, and have been, to us, that we may be thankful to God, and tender of them. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> That she was not wont to do so by him, and had never before crushed his foot, nor fallen down under him; he might therefore conclude there was something more than ordinary that made her do so now. Note, 1. The rare occurrence of an offence should moderate our displeasure against an offender. 2. When the creatures depart from their wonted obedience to us, we should enquire the cause within ourselves, and be humbled for our sin. <div eID="gen3144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3145" type="x-p"/> 2. Balaam at length had notice of God's displeasure by the angel, and this did startle him. When God opened his eyes <hi type="italic">he saw the angel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.22.31">v. 31</reference>), and then he himself <hi type="italic">fell flat upon his face,</hi> in reverence of that glorious messenger, and in fear of the sword he saw in his hand. God has many ways of breading and bringing down the hard and unhumbled heart. (1.) The angel reproved him for his outrageousness (<reference osisRef="Num.22.32-Num.22.33">v. 32, 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore hast thou smitten thy ass?</hi> Whether we consider it or no, it is certain that God will call us to account for the abuses done to his creatures. Nay, he shows him how much more reason he had to smite upon his breast, and to condemn himself, than to fly out thus against his ass ("<hi type="italic">Thy way is perverse before me,</hi> and then how canst thou expect to prosper?"), and how much wiser his ass was than himself, and how much beholden he was to her that she turned aside; it was for his safety, and not for her own, for had she gone on he had been slain, and she had been saved alive. Note, When our eyes are opened we shall see what danger we are in in a sinful way, and how much it was for our advantage to be crossed in it, and what fools we were to quarrel with our crosses which helped to save our lives. (2.) Balaam then seemed to relent (<reference osisRef="Num.22.34">v. 34</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have sinned,</hi> sinned in undertaking this journey, sinned in pushing on so violently;" but he excused it with this, that he saw not the angel; yet, now that he did see him, he was willing to go back again. That which was displeasing to God was not so much his going as his going with a malicious design against Israel, and a secret hope that notwithstanding the proviso with which his permission was clogged he might prevail to curse them, and so gratify Balak, and get preferment under him. It does not appear that he was sensible of this wickedness of his heart, or willing to own it, but, when he finds he cannot go forward, he will be content (since there is no remedy) to go back. Here is no sign that his heart is turned, but, if his hands are tied, he cannot help it. Thus many leave their sins only because their sins have left them. There seems to be a reformation of the life, but what will this avail if there be no renovation of the heart? (3.) The angel however continued his permission: "<hi type="italic">Go with the men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.22.35">v. 35</reference>. Go, if thou hast a mind to be made a fool of, and to be shamed before Balak, and all the princes of Moab. <hi type="italic">Go, only the word that I shall speak unto thee, that thou shalt speak,</hi> whether thou wilt or no," for this seems not to be a precept, but a prediction of the event, that he should not only not be able to curse Israel, but should be forced to bless them, which would be more for the glory of God and his own confusion than if he had turned back. Thus God gave him fair warning, but he would not take it; he <hi type="italic">went with the princes of Balak.</hi> For the iniquity of Balaam's covetousness God was wroth, and smote him, but he <hi type="italic">went on frowardly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.17">Isa. lvii. 17</reference>.
entries.ed7787780b90e5e5e7360f14d2732b2cf6c7cc57: <div eID="gen3145" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Meeting between Balak and Balaam. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1452.)</title> <div sID="gen3146" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> And when Balak heard that Balaam was come, he went out to meet him unto a city of Moab, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the border of Arnon, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the utmost coast. <hi type="super">37</hi> And Balak said unto Balaam, Did I not earnestly send unto thee to call thee? wherefore camest thou not unto me? am I not able indeed to promote thee to honour? <hi type="super">38</hi> And Balaam said unto Balak, Lo, I am come unto thee: have I now any power at all to say any thing? the word that God putteth in my mouth, that shall I speak. <hi type="super">39</hi> And Balaam went with Balak, and they came unto Kirjath-huzoth. 40 And Balak offered oxen and sheep, and sent to Balaam, and to the princes that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him. <hi type="super">41</hi> And it came to pass on the morrow, that Balak took Balaam, and brought him up into the high places of Baal, that thence he might see the utmost <hi type="italic">part</hi> of the people. <div eID="gen3146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3147" type="x-p"/> We have here the meeting between Balak and Balaam, confederate enemies to God's Israel; but here they seem to differ in their expectations of the success. 1. Balak speaks of it with confidence, not doubting but to gain his point now that Balaam had come. In expectation of this, he went out to meet him, even to the utmost border of his country (<reference osisRef="Num.22.36">v. 36</reference>), partly to gratify his own impatient desire to see one he had such great expectations from, and partly to do honour to Balaam, and so to engage him with his utmost power to serve him. See what respect heathen princes paid to those that had but the name and face of prophets, and pretended to have any interest in heaven; and how welcome one was that came with his mouth full of curses. What a shame is it then that the ambassadors of Christ are so little respected by most, so much despised by some, and that those are so coldly entertained who bring tidings of peace and a blessing! Balak has now nothing to complain of but that Balaam did not come sooner, <reference osisRef="Num.22.37">v. 37</reference>. And he thinks that he should have considered the importunity Balak had used, <hi type="italic">Did I not earnestly send to thee?</hi> (and the importunity of people inferior to kings has prevailed with many against their inclinations), and that he should also have considered Balak's intentions concerning him: <hi type="italic">Am not I able to promote thee to honour?</hi> Balak, as king, was in his own kingdom the fountain of honour, and Balaam should have his choice of all the preferments that were in his gift; he therefore thinks himself affronted by Balaam's delays, which looked as if he thought the honours he prepared not worthy his acceptance. Note, Promotion to honour is a very tempting bait to many people; and it were well if we would be drawn into the service of God by the honour he sets before us. Why do we delay to come unto him? Is <hi type="italic">not he able to promote us to honour?</hi> 2. Balaam speaks doubtfully of the issue, and bids Balak not depend to much upon him (<reference osisRef="Num.22.38">v. 38</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Have I now any power at all to say any thing?</hi> I have come, but what the nearer am I? Gladly would I curse Israel; but I must not, I cannot, God will not suffer me." He seems to speak with vexation at the hook in his nose and the bridle in his jaws, such as Sennacherib was tied up with, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Isa. xxxvii. 29</reference>. 3. They address themselves with all speed to the business. Balaam is nobly entertained over night, a sacrifice of thanksgiving is offered to the gods of Moab, for the safe arrival of this welcome guest, and his is treated with a feast upon the sacrifice, <reference osisRef="Num.22.40">v. 40</reference>. And the next morning, that no time might be lost, Balak takes Balaam in his chariot to the high places of his kingdom, not only because their holiness (such as it was), he thought, might give some advantage to his divinations, but their height might give him a convenient prospect of the camp of Israel, which was to be the butt or mark at which he must shoot his envenomed arrows. And now Balaam is really as solicitous to please Balak as ever he had pretended to be to please God. See what need we have to pray every day, <hi type="italic">Our Father in heaven, lead us not into temptation.</hi>  <chapter eID="Num.22"/> <div eID="gen3147" type="x-p"/>

entries.1fa3356d166557c2913be2587b7cce86ee680bbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1486"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.22.1-Num.22.20">Nu 22:1-20</reference>. Balak's First Message for Balaam Refused.</title> <div sID="gen1994" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1486"/><hi type="bold">1. Israel ... pitched in the plains of Moab--</hi>so called from having formerly belonged to that people, though wrested from them by Sihon. It was a dry, sunken, desert region on the east of the Jordan valley, opposite Jericho. <div eID="gen1994" type="x-p"/>
entries.eecf31dd00131aca4ae172d1de3d9f51bd44dc19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1487"/><div sID="gen1995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1487"/><hi type="bold">2. Balak--</hi>that is, "empty." Terrified (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.25">De 2:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Ex 15:15</reference>) at the approach of so vast a multitude and not daring to encounter them in the field, he resolved to secure their destruction by other means. <div eID="gen1995" type="x-p"/>
entries.d18ed527fd714efbacc33ff4fcd39569caba44dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1488"/><div sID="gen1996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1488"/><hi type="bold">4. elders of Midian--</hi>called kings (<reference osisRef="Num.31.8">Nu 31:8</reference>) and princes (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.21">Jos 13:21</reference>). The Midianites, a distinct people on the southern frontier of Moab, united with them as confederates against Israel, their common enemy. <div eID="gen1996" type="x-p"/>
entries.df8ab56203d477d6cd1cee44bee561330cd23655: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1489"/><div sID="gen1997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1489"/><hi type="bold">5. He sent messengers therefore unto Balaam--</hi>that is, "lord" or "devourer" of people, a famous soothsayer (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.22">Jos 13:22</reference>).<div eID="gen1997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">son of Beor--</hi>or, in the Chaldee form, Bosor--that is, "destruction."<div eID="gen1998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Pethor--</hi>a city of Mesopotamia, situated on the Euphrates. <div eID="gen1999" type="x-p"/>
entries.05c37a5c39e420ac419a3009899ef83a7595d03c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1490"/><div sID="gen2000" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1490"/><hi type="bold">6. Come ... curse me this people--</hi>Among the heathen an opinion prevailed that prayers for evil or curses would be heard by the unseen powers as well as prayers for good, when offered by a prophet or priest and accompanied by the use of certain rites. Many examples are found in the histories of the Greeks and Romans of whole armies being devoted to destruction, and they occur among the natives of India and other heathen countries still. In the Burmese war, magicians were employed to curse the British troops. <div eID="gen2000" type="x-p"/>
entries.5673b923bfe38db6aa40012a516fcdd2acc6aa52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1491"/><div sID="gen2001" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1491"/><hi type="bold">7. the elders of Moab and ... of Midian departed with the rewards of divination--</hi>like the fee of a fortune teller, and being a royal present, it would be something handsome. <div eID="gen2001" type="x-p"/>
entries.f76d9b2c2cea40f6c240b5f496c7959b009e32cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1492"/><div sID="gen2002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1492"/><hi type="bold">8-14. Lodge here this night, and I will bring you word again, as the Lord shall speak unto me, &c.--</hi>God usually revealed His will in visions and dreams; and Balaam's birth and residence in Mesopotamia, where the remains of patriarchal religion still lingered, account for his knowledge of the true God. His real character has long been a subject of discussion. Some, judging from his language, have thought him a saint; others, looking to his conduct, have described him as an irreligious charlatan; and a third class consider him a novice in the faith, who had a fear of God, but who had not acquired power over his passions [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen2002" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a30ec525d720814ae35fbe3250c7392a9f8351e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1494"/><div sID="gen2004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1494"/><hi type="bold">19-20. tarry ye also here this night, that I may know what the Lord will say unto me more--</hi>The divine will, as formerly declared, not being according to his desires, he hoped by a second request to bend it, as he had already bent his own conscience, to his ruling passions of pride and covetousness. The permission granted to Balaam is in accordance with the ordinary procedure of Providence. God often gives up men to follow the impulse of their own lusts; but there is no approval in thus leaving them to act at the prompting of their own wicked hearts (<reference osisRef="Josh.13.27">Jos 13:27</reference>). <div eID="gen2004" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae3ca526b2a149e59cdaa9753df2ce67e1a74c73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1495"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Num.22.21-Num.22.41">Nu 22:21-41</reference>. The Journey.</title> <div sID="gen2005" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1495"/><hi type="bold">21. Balaam ... saddled his ass--</hi>probably one of the white sprightly animals which persons of rank were accustomed to ride. The saddle, as usually in the East, would be nothing more than a pad or his outer cloak. <div eID="gen2005" type="x-p"/>
entries.aaaab99852178337adb1170f972f6a4719f22417: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1496"/><div sID="gen2006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1496"/><hi type="bold">22. God's anger was kindled because he went--</hi>The displeasure arose partly from his neglecting the condition on which leave was granted him--namely, to wait till the princes of Moab "came to call him" [Nu 22:20], and because, through desire for "the wages of unrighteousness" [2Pe 2:15], he entertained the secret purpose of acting in opposition to the solemn charge of God. <div eID="gen2006" type="x-p"/>
entries.23ec87b50b9081b194424a6dfa0ed5b683bb4190: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1497"/><div sID="gen2007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1497"/><hi type="bold">24. the angel of the Lord stood in a path of the vineyards--</hi>The roads which lead through fields and vineyards are so narrow that in most parts a man could not pass a beast without care and caution. A stone or mud fence flanks each side of these roads, to prevent the soil being washed off by the rains. <div eID="gen2007" type="x-p"/>
entries.e283c7d11864e35b4ec0f45688bc4a4cdbcccd83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1498"/><div sID="gen2008" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1498"/><hi type="bold">28. the Lord opened the mouth of the ass--</hi>to utter, like a parrot, articulate sounds, without understanding them. That this was a visionary scene is a notion which seems inadmissible, because of the improbability of a vision being described as an actual occurrence in the middle of a plain history. Besides, the opening of the ass's mouth must have been an external act, and that, with the manifest tenor of Peter's language, strongly favors the literal view [2Pe 2:15, 16]. The absence of any surprise at such a phenomenon on the part of Balaam may be accounted for by his mind being wholly engrossed with the prospect of gain, which produced "the madness of the prophet" [2Pe 2:16]. "It was a miracle, wrought to humble his proud heart, which had to be first subjected in the school of an ass before he was brought to attend to the voice of God speaking by the angel" [Calvin]. <div eID="gen2008" type="x-p"/>
entries.99b5f671b84e56673bfa1e267107c11704cf08df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1499"/><div sID="gen2009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1499"/><hi type="bold">34-35. I have sinned ... if it displease thee, I will get me back again--</hi>Notwithstanding this confession, he evinced no spirit of penitence, as he speaks of desisting only from the outward act. entries.67d0d00b5f66269845b23ffd522cb33287a85ef8: <div eID="gen5917" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen5918" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5919" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5919" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5918" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5920" type="x-p"/> The Israelites pitch in the plains of Moab, <reference osisRef="Num.22.1">Num 22:1</reference>. Balak, king of Moab, is greatly terrified, <reference osisRef="Num.22.2-Num.22.4">Num 22:2-4</reference>; and sends to Balaam, a diviner, to come and curse them, <reference osisRef="Num.22.5">Num 22:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.22.6">Num 22:6</reference>. The elders of Moab take a reward and carry it to Balaam, <reference osisRef="Num.22.7">Num 22:7</reference>. He inquires of the Lord, and is positively ordered not to go with them, <reference osisRef="Num.22.8-Num.22.12">Num 22:8-12</reference>. He communicates this to the elders of Moab, <reference osisRef="Num.22.13">Num 22:13</reference>. They return to Balak with this information, <reference osisRef="Num.22.14">Num 22:14</reference>. He sends some of his princes to Balaam with promises of great honor, <reference osisRef="Num.22.15-Num.22.17">Num 22:15-17</reference>. He consults God, and is permitted! to go, on certain conditions, <reference osisRef="Num.22.18-Num.22.20">Num 22:18-20</reference>. Balaam sets off, is opposed by an angel of the Lord, and the Lord miraculously opens the mouth of his ass to reprove him, <reference osisRef="Num.22.21-Num.22.30">Num 22:21-30</reference>. Balaam sees the angel, and is reproved by him, <reference osisRef="Num.22.31-Num.22.33">Num 22:31-33</reference>. He humbles himself, and offers to go back, <reference osisRef="Num.22.34">Num 22:34</reference>; but is ordered to proceed, on the same conditions as before, <reference osisRef="Num.22.35">Num 22:35</reference>. The king of Moab goes out to meet him, <reference osisRef="Num.22.36">Num 22:36</reference>. His address to him, <reference osisRef="Num.22.37">Num 22:37</reference>. Balaam's firm answer, <reference osisRef="Num.22.38">Num 22:38</reference>. Balak sacrifices, and takes Balaam to the high places of Baal, that he may see the whole of the Israelitish camp, <reference osisRef="Num.22.39-Num.22.41">Num 22:39-41</reference>. <div eID="gen5920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5921" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen5921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5922" type="x-p"/> And pitched in the plains of Moab - They had taken no part of the country that at present appertained to the Moabites; they had taken only that part which had formerly belonged to this people, but had been taken from them by Sihon, king of the Amorites. <div eID="gen5922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5923" type="x-p"/> On this side Jordan - On the east side. By Jericho, that is, over against it.
entries.5585c8e2f4abdb7fae71b7e1943f588ab085d55c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen5923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5924" type="x-p"/> To Pethor, which is by the river of the land of the children of his people - Dr. Kennicott justly remarks, that "the description now given of Balaam's residence, instead of being particular, agrees with any place in any country where there is a river; for he lived by Pethor, which is by the river of the land of the children of his people. But was Pethor then near the Nile in Egypt? Or in Canaan, near Jordan? Or in Mesopotamia, near the Euphrates, and belonging to the Ammonites? This last was in fact the case; and therefore it is well that twelve Hebrew MSS. (with two of De Rossi's) confirm the Samaritan text here in reading, instead of עמו ammo, his people, עמון Ammon, with the Syriac and Vulgate versions." Houbigant properly contends for this reading; and necessity urges the propriety of adopting it. It should therefore stand thus: by the river of the land of the children of Ammon; and thus it agrees with <reference osisRef="Deu.23.4">Deu 23:4</reference>.
entries.610c0cf472b2b337fa8675ac10597ba0bceeabe6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen5924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5925" type="x-p"/> Come now, therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people - Balaam, once a prophet of the true God, appears to have been one of the Moshelim, (see <reference osisRef="Num.21.27">Num 21:27</reference>), who had added to his poetic gift that of sorcery or divination. It was supposed that prophets and sorcerers had a power to curse persons and places so as to confound all their designs, frustrate their counsels, enervate their strength, and fill them with fear, terror, and dismay. See <reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Gen 9:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.109.6">Psa 109:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.109.20">Psa 109:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jos.6.26">Jos 6:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.5">Jer 17:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.6">Jer 17:6</reference>. <div eID="gen5925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5926" type="x-p"/> Macrobius has a whole chapter De carmine quo evocari solebant dii tutelares, et aut urbes, aut exercitus devoveri. "Of the incantations which were used to induce the tutelary gods to forsake the cities, etc., over which they presided, and to devote cities and whole armies to destruction." See Saturnal., lib. iii., cap. ix. He gives us two of the ancient forms used in reference to the destruction of Carthage; the first, to call over the protecting deities, was pronounced by the dictator or general, and none other, when they began the siege. It is as follows, literatim et punctatim: - <div eID="gen5926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5927" type="x-p"/> Si. Deus. si. Dea. est. cui. popolus. civitas. que. Karthaginiensis. est in. tutela. te. que. maxime, ille. qui. urbis. hujus. popoli. que. tutelam. recepisti. precor. veneror, que. veniam. que. a. vobis. peto. ut. vos. popolum. civitatem. que. Karthaginiensem. deseratis. loca. templa. sacra. urbem. que. eorum. relinquatis. absque. his. abeatis. ei. que. popolo. civitati. que. metum. formidinem. oblivionem. injiciatis. proditi. que. Romam. ad. me. meos. que. veniatis. nostra. que. vobis. loca. templa. sacra. urbs. acceptior. probatior. que. sit. mihi. que. popolo. que. Romano. militibus. que. meis. praepositi. sitis. ut. sciamus. intelligamus. que. Si. ita. feceritis. voveo. vobis. templa. ludos. que. facturum. "Whether it be god or goddess, under whose protection the people and city of Carthage are placed; and thee, especially, who hast undertaken to defend this city and people; I pray, beseech, and earnestly entreat that you would forsake the people and city of Carthage, and leave their places, temples, sacred things, and city, and depart from them: and that you would inspire this people and city with fear, terror, and forgetfulness: and that, coming out from them, you would pass over to Rome, to me, and to mine: and that our places, temples, sacred things, and city may be more agreeable and more acceptable to you: and that you would preside over me, the Roman people, and my soldiers; that we may know and perceive it. If ye will do this, I promise to consecrate to your honor both temples and games." <div eID="gen5927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5928" type="x-p"/> The second, to devote the city to destruction, which it was supposed the tutelary gods had abandoned, is the following: <div eID="gen5928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5929" type="x-p"/> Dis. Pater. Vejovis. Manes. sive. vos. quo. allo. nomine. fas. est. nominare. ut. omnes. iliam. urbem. Karthaginem. exercitum. que. quem. ego. me. sentio. dicere. fuga. formidine. terrore. que. compleatis. qui. que. adversum. legiones. exercitum. que. nostrum. arma. tela. que. ferent. Uti. vos. eum. exercitum. eos. hostes. eos. que. homines. urbes. agros. que. eorum. et. qui. in. his. locis. regionibus. que. agris. urbibus. ve. habitant. abducatis. lumine. supero. privetis. exercitum. que. hostium. urbes. agros. que. eorum. quos. me. sentio. dicere. uti. vos. eas. urbes. agros. que. capita. aetates. que. eorum. devotas. consecratas. que. habeatis. illis. legibus. quibus. quando. que. sunt. maxime. hostes. devoti. eos. que. ego. vicarios. pro. me. fide. magistratu. que. meo. pro. popolo. Romano. exercitibus. legionibus. que. nostris. do. devoveo. ut. me. meam. que. fidem. imperium. que. legiones. exercitum. que. nostrum. qui. in. his. rebus. gerundis. sunt. bene. salvos. siritis. esse. Si. haec. ita. faxitis. ut. ego. sciam. sentiam. intelligam. que. tune. quisquis. hoc. votum. faxit. ubi. ubi. faxit. recte. factum. esto. ovibus. atris. tribus. Tellus. mater. te. que. Juppiter. obtestor. "Dis. Pater. Vejosis. Manes., or by whatsoever name you wish to be invoked, I pray you to fill this city of Carthage with fear and terror; and to put that army to flight which I mention, and which bears arms or darts against Our legions and armies: and that ye may take away this army, those enemies, those men, their cities and their country, and all who dwell in those places, regions, countries, or cities; and deprive them of the light above: and let all their armies, cities, country, chiefs, and people be held by you consecrated and devoted, according to those laws by which, and at what time, enemies can be most effectually devoted. I also give and devote them as vicarious sacrifices for myself and my magistracy; for the Roman people, and for all our armies and legions; and for the whole empire, and that all the armies and legions which are employed in these countries may be preserved in safety. If therefore ye will do these things, as I know, conceive, and intend, then he who makes this vow wheresoever and whensoever he shall make it, I engage shall sacrifice three black sheep to thee, O mother Earth, and to thee. O Jupiter." "When the execrator mentions the earth, he stoops down and places both his hands on it; and when he names Jupiter, he lifts up both his hands to heaven; and when he mentions his vow, he places his hands upon his breast." Among the ancient records, Macrobius says he found many cities and people devoted in this way. The Romans held that no city could be taken till its tutelary god had forsaken it; or if it could be taken, it would be unlawful, as it would be sacrilegious to have the gods in captivity. They therefore endeavored to persuade the gods of their enemies to come over to their party. Virgil intimates that Troy was destroyed, only because the tutelary gods had forsaken it: - <div eID="gen5929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5930" type="x-p"/> Excessere omnes, adytis arisque relictis, <div eID="gen5930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5931" type="x-p"/> Dii, quibus imperium hoc steterat. <div eID="gen5931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5932" type="x-p"/> Aen., lib. ii., ver. 351. "All the gods, by whose assistance the empire had hitherto been preserved, forsook their altars and their temples." <div eID="gen5932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5933" type="x-p"/> And it was on this account that the Greeks employed all their artifice to steal away the Palladium, on which they believed the safety of Troy depended. <div eID="gen5933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5934" type="x-p"/> Tacitus observes that when Suetonius Paulinus prepared his army to cross over into Mona, (Anglesea), where the Britons and Druids made their last stand, the priestesses, with dishevelled hair, white vestments, and torches in their hands, ran about like furies, devoting their enemies to destruction; and he farther adds that the sight, the attitude, and horrible imprecations of these priestesses had such effect on the Roman soldiers, that for a while they stood still and suffered themselves to be pierced with the darts of the Britons, without making any resistance. Tacit. Ann., l. xiv., c. 29. Many accounts are related in the Hindoo Pooran of kings employing sages to curse their enemies when too powerful for them - Ward's Customs. <div eID="gen5934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5935" type="x-p"/> The Jews also had a most horrible form of execration, as may be seen in Buxtorf's Talmudical Lexicon under the word תדם. These observations and authorities, drawn out in so much detail, are necessary to cast light on the strange and curious history related in this and the two following chapters.
entries.ff80f74acdac11dc11ab0499ed47801b5013a4e2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen5935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5936" type="x-p"/> The rewards of divination - Whoever went to consult a prophet took with him a present, as it was on such gratuitous offerings the prophets lived; but here more than a mere present is intended, perhaps every thing necessary to provide materials for the incantation. The drugs, etc., used on such occasions were often very expensive. It appears that Balaam was very covetous, and that he loved the wages of unrighteousness, and probably lived by it; see <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.15">2Pet 2:15</reference>.
entries.15eec8b88c1fde993d3926c8cdc2ab39c0cdfbe6: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen5936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5937" type="x-p"/> I will bring you word again, as the Lord shall speak - So it appears he knew the true God, and had been in the habit of consulting him, and receiving oracles from his mouth.
entries.030114dcf2d6083a71dbc75729fcfe76f5d622df: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen5937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5938" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people - That is, Thou shalt not go with them to curse the people. With them he might go, as we find he afterwards did by God's own command, but not to curse the people; this was wholly forbidden. Probably the command, Thou shalt not go, refers here to that time, viz., the first invitation: and in this sense it was most punctually obeyed by Balaam; see <reference osisRef="Num.22.13">Num 22:13</reference>.
entries.eb9c52a708108d9577b56026944e7f8633a74ff4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen5938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5939" type="x-p"/> Balaam refuseth to come with us - "Observe," says Mr. Ainsworth, "Satan's practice against God's word, seeking to lessen the same, and that from hand to hand, till he bring it to naught. Balaam told the princes less than God told him, and they relate to Balak less than Balaam told them; so that when the answer came to the king of Moab, it was not the word of God, but the word of man; it was simply, Balaam refuseth to come, without ever intimating that God had forbidden him." But in this Balaam is not to blame; he told the messengers in the most positive manner, Jehovah refuseth to give me leave to go with you, <reference osisRef="Num.22.13">Num 22:13</reference>; and more explicit he could not be.
entries.3f6771af8b687f43029ae635c5353433f3891dea: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen5939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5940" type="x-p"/> I cannot go beyond the word of the Lord my God - Balaam knew God too well to suppose he could reverse any of his purposes; and he respected him too much to attempt to do any thing without his permission. Though he was covetous, yet he dared not, even when strongly tempted both by riches and honors, to go contrary to the command of his God. Many make all the professions of Balaam, without justifying them by their conduct. "They pretend," says one, "they would not do any thing against the word of God for a house full of gold, and yet will do it for a handful!"
entries.7ea3d0cf2f398836e9c16ec3689d944e7a7856be: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen5940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5941" type="x-p"/> What the Lord will say unto me more - He did not know but God might make a farther discovery of his will to him, and therefore he might very innocently seek farther information.
entries.37fab939a7f019019fd20fa5f4f5f7d8419913e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen5941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5942" type="x-p"/> If the men come - go with them - This is a confirmation of what was observed on the twelfth verse; though we find his going was marked with the Divine displeasure, because he wished, for the sake of the honors and rewards, to fulfill as far as possible the will of the king of Moab. Mr. Shuckford observes that the pronoun הוא hu is sometimes used to denote a person's doing a thing out of his own head, without regard to the directions of another. Thus in the case of Balaam, when God had allowed him to go with the messengers of Balak, if they came in the morning to call him; because he was more hasty than he ought to have been, and went to them instead of staying till they should come to him, it was said of him, not כי הלך ki halach, that he went, but כי הולך הוא ki holech hu, i. e., he went of his own head - without being called; and in this, Mr. Shuckford supposes, his iniquity chiefly lay - Connex., vol. iii., p. 115. How many are restrained from sinning, merely through the fear of God! They would gladly do the evil, but it is forbidden on awful penalties; they wish the thing were not prohibited for they have a strong desire to do it.
entries.345baaf1d1ec76f83f8601e75c2aae74a7ccd1f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen5942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5943" type="x-p"/> And the ass saw the angel - When God granted visions those alone who were particularly interested saw them while others in the same company saw nothing; see <reference osisRef="Dan.10.7">Dan 10:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.9.7">Act 9:7</reference>.
entries.9e090156b892ca3c3908d5ef3703c4687112c11a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen5943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5944" type="x-p"/> And the angel - stood in a narrow place - In this carriage of the angel says Mr. Ainsworth the Lord shows us the proceedings of his judgments against sinners: First he mildly shakes his rod at them but lets them go untouched. Secondly he comes nearer and touches them with an easy correction as it were wringing their foot against the wall. Thirdly, when all this is ineffectual, he brings them into such straits, that they can neither turn to the right hand nor to the left, but must fall before his judgments, if they do not fully turn to him.
entries.8c9d267caea653ee05245d46b260a90bc883a6a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen5944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5945" type="x-p"/> The Lord opened the mouth of the ass - And where is the wonder of all this? If the ass had opened her own mouth, and reproved the rash prophet, we might well be astonished; but when God opens the mouth, an ass can speak as well as a man. It is worthy of remark here, that Balaam testifies no surprise at this miracle, because he saw it was the Lord's doing. Of animate and inanimate things receiving for a short time the gift of speech, the heathen mythology furnishes many fictitious examples, with which I do not deem it proper to occupy the reader's time.
entries.fc8f9990e6f3619a9c5f180054943a78ac3d1e08: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen5945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5946" type="x-p"/> Surely now also I had slain thee - How often are the meanest animals, and the most trivial occurrences, instruments of the preservation of our lives, and of the salvation of our souls! The messenger of justice would have killed Balaam, had not the mercy of God prevented the ass from proceeding.
entries.9db2bb6aa6f04af372005df07df1501f9fddf89e: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen5946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5947" type="x-p"/> If it displease thee, I will get me back again - Here is a proof, that though he loved the wages of unrighteousness, yet he still feared God; and he is now willing to drop the enterprise if God be displeased with his proceeding. The piety of many called Christians does not extend thus far; they see that the thing displeases God, and yet they proceed. Reader, is this thy case?
entries.a83fff1f6db83a153b281d27f09b6d197484687d: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen5947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5948" type="x-p"/> The word that God putteth in my mouth, that shall I speak - Here was a noble resolution, and he was certainly faithful to it: though he wished to please the king, and get wealth and honor, yet he would not displease God to realize even these bright prospects. Many who slander this poor semi-antinomian prophet, have not half his piety.
entries.2012866c20d44d1775a4bee4cdc333aa322c868f: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen5948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5949" type="x-p"/> And Balak offered oxen, etc. - This was to gain the favor of his gods, and perhaps to propitiate Jehovah, that the end for which he had sent for Balaam might be accomplished.
entries.0c91a8b9b97cc0781e527ebae0a3fd7782cfdfd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen5949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5950" type="x-p"/> That - he might see the utmost part of the people - As he thought Balaam must have them all in his eye when he pronounced his curse, lest it might not extend to those who were not in sight. On this account he took him up into the high places of Baal.  <chapter eID="Num.22"/> <div eID="gen5950" type="x-p"/>

entries.bedcb7173a4b7179a158b843c953bdd4950b2755: Num 22:1 <div eID="gen1897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1898" type="x-p"/> After the defeat of the two Amorite kings, Sihon and Og, and the conquest of their kingdoms in Gilead and Bashan, the Israelites removed from the height of Pisgah, on the mountains of Abarim before Nebo (see at Num 21:20), and encamped in the “<hi type="italic">Arboth</hi> <hi type="italic">Moab </hi>(the steppes of Moab), on the other side of the Jordan of Jericho,” i.e., that part of the Jordan which skirted the province of Jericho. <hi type="italic">Arboth Moab</hi> was the name given to that portion of the Arabah, or large plain of the Jordan, the present <hi type="italic">Ghor</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.1.1">Deu 1:1</reference>), which belonged to the territory of the Moabites previous to the spread of the Amorites under Sihon in the land to the east of the Jordan, and which probably reached from the Dead Sea to the mouth of the Jabbok. The site of the Israelitish camp is therefore defined with greater minuteness by the clause “beyond the Jordan of Jericho.” This place of encampment, which is frequently alluded to (Num 26:3, Num 26:63; Num 31:12; Num 33:48, Num 33:50; Num 35:1; Num 36:13; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.32">Jos 13:32</reference>), extended, according to Num 33:49, from <hi type="italic">Beth-jeshimoth</hi> to <hi type="italic">Abel-shittim</hi>. <hi type="italic">Beth-jeshimoth</hi> (i.e., house of wastes), on the north-eastern desert border (<hi type="italic">Jeishimon</hi>, Num 21:20) of the Dead Sea, a town allotted to the tribe of Reuben (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.3">Jos 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.13.20">Jos 13:20</reference>), was situated, according to the <hi type="italic">Onom</hi>. (s. v<hi type="italic">.</hi>Beethasimou'th<hi type="italic">, Bethsimuth</hi>), ten Roman miles, or four hours, to the south (S.E.) of Jericho, on the Dead Sea; according to <hi type="italic">Josephus</hi> (<hi type="italic">bell. jud</hi>. iv. 7, 6), it was to the south of <hi type="italic">Julias</hi> (<hi type="italic">Livias</hi>), i.e., <hi type="italic">Beth-haram, or Rameh</hi>, on the northern edge of the Wady Hesban (see at Num 32:36), or in the <hi type="italic">Ghor el Seisabân</hi>, on the northern coast of the Dead Sea, and the southern end of the plain of the Jordan. <hi type="italic">Abel Shittim</hi> (השּׁטּים אבל), i.e., the acacia-meadow, or, in its briefer form, <hi type="italic">Shittim</hi> (Num 35:1), was situated, according to Josephus (Ant. iv. 8, 1), on the same spot as the later town of <hi type="italic">Abila</hi>, in a locality rich in date-palms, sixty stadia from the Jordan, probably by the Wady <hi type="italic">Eshtah</hi> to the north of the Wady Hesban; even if <hi type="italic">Knobel's</hi> supposition that the name is connected with אשׁטה = שׁטּה with א <hi type="italic">prost</hi>. should not be a tenable one. From <hi type="italic">Shittim</hi> or <hi type="italic">Sittim</hi> the Israelites advanced, under Joshua, to the Jordan, to effect the conquest of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.3.1">Jos 3:1</reference>). <div eID="gen1898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1899" type="x-p"/> In the steppes of Moab the Israelites encamped upon the border of the promised land, from which they were only separated by the Jordan.
